e-5528.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvalue of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvector
e-5528.problem:
Determine whether ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/59af73d1cda1a988c775ccf198b53653b96660b4ad8416add1b0c1816e89a5a5.png) is an eigenvector of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/963bcaf94bc481fe8fbc99ca28fba037047d8821661eadcf0e5e9ce50ba39ef8.png)
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
e-5528.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $\mathbf{v}$ such that $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 8 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18+6\text{i} \\ 24\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18{\text{i}}^{2}+6\text{i} \\ 24\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\text{i}[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A\mathbf{v} = 6\textrm{i} \mathbf{v},$ we conclude that $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda=6\textrm{i}.$

e-5527.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvector of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvalue
e-5527.problem:
Find an eigenvector of 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/6e4a720878567b81cb593aa5a9bfc5aa2c8c7ace61d111bb8934bc94056c04bc.png)
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-3+4\textrm{i}.$
e-5527.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-3+4\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-3+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -3+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 4 \\ -4 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4\text{i}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}-4\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-3+4\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
x_1 = -\textrm{i}x_2.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/0d2e7b9f7011624cf74762419efd784144cf41e2000301d093e1aa612e96f495.png)

Setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/2e4bc467e9fbc15574d2739766eada3f297500ecf1a69382500271751b2edf65.png)

e-5529.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Complex Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
e-5529.problem:
Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/07f01e2a202e29fee28a98d386df1d22fd21efcf1ee4d0a6a4cc56f9b637d57c.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/a547975b3524322daec753a8ddd010e50e815307d72bc07933d1e3674b4b462c.png) be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/53de45d6b1504ec53ca81471731b06ac5524a12230f0414553624c116a6f47c6.png)
Given that $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of ${\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}}.$
e-5529.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda_1 =4+5\textrm{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 4+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-5\text{i}{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}-5\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(4+5\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = \textrm{i}x_1.
$$

So, the general solution is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/b212192b142e9b4686a4d39e5957db5f3bfbca6283bfcb1d88a6fc57a4a27848.png)

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/65c073a60a27234349281e873958c2c9d54fb703331a4de23cc358a3eab1b232.png) 

Now, since $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of $\lambda_1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\lambda_2=\overline{\lambda_1}=4-5\textrm{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector must be the complex conjugate of $\mathbf v_1.$ Therefore, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/ca11ae0cca8d07c026108e71b96398171597f7330cb2390d871a8071e7bba873.png)

Finally, we obtain

$$
{\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}} = {\dfrac{(1)(1)}{(\textrm{i})(-\textrm{i})}} = 1.
$$

$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 \\ -8 & 4\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
after.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors are non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 \\ -8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4-4\text{i} \\ -8\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4{\text{i}}^{2}-4\text{i} \\ -8\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4\text{i}[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=-4\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-4\text{i}.$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Determine whether $v=[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 9 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
after.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 9 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9+6\text{i} \\ 2-3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9{\text{i}}^{2}+6\text{i} \\ 2-3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\text{i}(2-3\text{i}) \\ 1(2-3\text{i})\end{aligned}] \\  & =(2-3\text{i})[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =(2-3\text{i})v.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvalue of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvector
content.problem:
Determine whether $v=[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 9 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
content.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 9 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9+6\text{i} \\ 2-3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9{\text{i}}^{2}+6\text{i} \\ 2-3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\text{i}(2-3\text{i}) \\ 1(2-3\text{i})\end{aligned}] \\  & =(2-3\text{i})[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =(2-3\text{i})v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=(2-3\text{i})v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2-3\text{i}.$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Determine whether $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
after.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6\text{i} \\ 6-6\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6\text{i} \\ -6{\text{i}}^{2}-6\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =3\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =3\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=3\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =3\text{i}.$

Question 6
?

If v=[ab] is an eigenvector of A=[35−21] that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=2+3i, then what is the value of ab?

a
−12+32i
b
1−3i
c
12−32i
d
−12−32i
e
12+32i
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=2+3i, and

A−λI=[35−21]−[2+3i002+3i]=[1−3i5−2−1−3i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(1−3i)x1+5x2=0−2x1+(−1−3i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(2+3i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

x1=−12(1+3i)x2

Therefore, the general solution is given by

[−12(1+3i)x2x2],x2∈C.

Setting x2=−2, we get the eigenvector

v=[1+3i−2].

Finally, ab=−1+3i2=−12−32i.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{5}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =\sqrt{5}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-\sqrt{5}\text{i} & 3 \\ -3 & -2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+(-2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-\sqrt{5}\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}(2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}(2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2+\sqrt{5}\text{i} \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-3}{2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}}=\frac{-3(2-\sqrt{5}\text{i})}{9}=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\text{i}.$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvector of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvalue
content.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{5}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
content.worked_solution:

(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-\sqrt{5}\text{i} & 3 \\ -3 & -2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}10 & 4 \\ -26 & -10\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-2\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 4 \\ -26 & -10\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10+2\text{i} & 4 \\ -26 & -10+2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(10+2\text{i}){x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -26{x}_{1}+(-10+2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A+2\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}(5+\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{1}{2}(5+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{5+\text{i}}{-2}=-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}.$

content.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}10 & 4 \\ -26 & -10\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-2\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 4 \\ -26 & -10\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10+2\text{i} & 4 \\ -26 & -10+2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(10+2\text{i}){x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -26{x}_{1}+(-10+2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A+2\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}(5+\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{1}{2}(5+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{5+\text{i}}{-2}=-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}.$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -5 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -5 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3+\text{i} & -5 \\ 2 & 3+\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-3+\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+(3+\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A+\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{5}(-3+\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{5}(-3+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-3+\text{i}}{5}=-\frac{3}{5}+\frac{1}{5}\text{i}.$

Question 10
?

If v=[ab] is an eigenvector of A=[−3−523] that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=−i, then what is the value of ba?

a
25−15i
b
−35+15i
c
35+15i
d
32−12i
e
−32+12i
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=−i, and

A−λI=[−3−523]−[−i00−i]=[−3+i−523+i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(−3+i)x1−5x2=02x1+(3+i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A+iI is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

x2=15(−3+i)x1

Therefore, the general solution is given by

[x115(−3+i)x1],x1∈C.

Setting x1=5, we get the eigenvector

v=[5−3+i].

Finally, ba=−3+i5=−35+15i.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvector of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvalue
content.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -5 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -5 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3+\text{i} & -5 \\ 2 & 3+\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-3+\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+(3+\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A+\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{5}(-3+\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{5}(-3+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-3+\text{i}}{5}=-\frac{3}{5}+\frac{1}{5}\text{i}.$

before.html:
Question 11
?

Let v1=[a1b1] and v2=[a2b2] be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−15−21]. Given that λ1=3i is an eigenvalue of A, find the value of a1a2b1b2.

a
10
b
5
c
52
d
3i
e
2i
Submit

decision.explanation: The eigenvalues are 3i and -3i, each with a one-dimensional eigenspace, so independent eigenvectors correspond to different eigenvalues. The second row gives a/b=(1-λ)/2. Thus (a₁a₂)/(b₁b₂)=(1-3i)(1+3i)/4=10/4=5/2. Both b components are nonzero because b=0 would force a=0.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -2 & 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-3\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{5}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{5}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=-3\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(5)(5)}{(1+3\text{i})(1-3\text{i})}=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

Question 11
?

Let v1=[a1b1] and v2=[a2b2] be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−15−21]. Given that λ1=3i is an eigenvalue of A, find the value of a1a2b1b2.

a
10
b
5
c
52
d
3i
e
2i
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ1=3i and

A−λ1I=[−15−21]−[3i003i]=[−1−3i5−21−3i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(−1−3i)x1+5x2=0−2x1+(1−3i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−3iI is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

x2=15(1+3i)x1

Hence, the general solution is given by

[x115(1+3i)x1],x1∈C.

Setting x1=5, we get the eigenvector

v1=[51+3i].

On the other hand, since λ1=3i is a complex eigenvalue of A, the second eigenvalue of A must be the complex conjugate of λ1. Therefore,

λ2=λ1―=−3i.

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to λ2 is

v2=v―1=[51−3i].

Therefore, we obtain

a1a2b1b2=(5)(5)(1+3i)(1−3i)=52.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Complex Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -2 & 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-3\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{5}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{5}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=-3\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(5)(5)}{(1+3\text{i})(1-3\text{i})}=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

Question 12
?

Let v1=[a1b1] and v2=[a2b2] be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−4−5106]. Given that λ1=1+5i is an eigenvalue of A, find the value of a1a2b1b2.

a
12
b
16
c
15
d
13
e
14
Submit

decision.explanation: The eigenvalues are 1+5i and 1-5i. Their eigenspaces are one-dimensional, so independent eigenvectors correspond to these different eigenvalues. From 10a+6b=λb, a/b=(λ-6)/10, giving ratios (-1+i)/2 and (-1-i)/2. Their product is (1+1)/4=1/2. Each b is nonzero, since b=0 would force a=0.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 10 & 6\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 10 & 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5-5\text{i} & -5 \\ 10 & 5-5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-5-5\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 10{x}_{1}+(5-5\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+5\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=1-5\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})}{(-2)(-2)}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Let v1=[a1b1] and v2=[a2b2] be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−4−5106]. Given that λ1=1+5i is an eigenvalue of A, find the value of a1a2b1b2.

a
12
b
16
c
15
d
13
e
14
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ1=1+5i and

A−λ1I=[−4−5106]−[1+5i001+5i]=[−5−5i−5105−5i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(−5−5i)x1−5x2=010x1+(5−5i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(1+5i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

x1=−12(1−i)x2

Hence, the general solution is given by

[−12(1−i)x2x2],x2∈C.

Setting x2=−2, we get the eigenvector

v1=[1−i−2].

On the other hand, since λ1=1+5i is a complex eigenvalue of A, the second eigenvalue of A must be the complex conjugate of λ1. Therefore,

λ2=λ1―=1−5i.

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to λ2 is

v2=v―1=[1+i−2].

Therefore, we obtain

a1a2b1b2=(1−i)(1+i)(−2)(−2)=12.

verification.explanation: Independent eigenvectors correspond to the distinct eigenvalues 1+5i and 1-5i. From 10a+6b=λb, their a/b ratios are (-1+i)/2 and (-1-i)/2. Multiplying gives 2/4=1/2, confirming the worked solution. Scaling either eigenvector does not change this ratio.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Complex Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 10 & 6\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 10 & 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5-5\text{i} & -5 \\ 10 & 5-5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-5-5\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 10{x}_{1}+(5-5\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+5\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=1-5\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})}{(-2)(-2)}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

$$

$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}(6+3\text{i}){x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -15{x}_{1}+(-6+3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-2+\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-2+\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.

$$
{\text{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=1+3\text{i}.
$$

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2-\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}=\frac{(5)(5)}{(-2+\text{i})(-2-\text{i})}=5.

decision.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is λ²+4λ+8, giving distinct eigenvalues -2±2i. Independent eigenvectors correspond to these different eigenvalues. From 5a+2b=λb, a/b=(λ-2)/5=(-4±2i)/5. Thus (a₁a₂)/(b₁b₂)=(16+4)/25=4/5. Each b is nonzero because b=0 would force a=0.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & -4 \\ 5 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-(-4)(5) & =0 \\ -12+6\lambda -2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm \sqrt{{4}^{2}-4(1)(8)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm 4\text{i}}{2} \\  & =-2\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =-2\pm 2\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+2\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4-2\text{i} & -4 \\ 5 & 4-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-4-2\text{i}){x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(4-2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-2+2\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-1-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-1-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2-2\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(2)(2)}{(-2-\text{i})(-2+\text{i})}=\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
